paper_b.title: On the Uniform Convergence of Relative Frequencies of Events to Their Probabilities

metadata.description: Parallel rediscovery: Vapnik-Chervonenkis (1971) establishes distribution-free uniform convergence of empirical to true probabilities for an event class with polynomial growth function, and gives the matching sample-complexity bound. Valiant (1984), apparently unaware of VC, develops the PAC framework for Boolean concept classes, obtaining the same kind of probabilistic approximation guarantees by counting concrete hypothesis classes (k-CNF, monotone DNF, mu-expressions) and applying Chernoff/coupon-collector arguments. The two share the core uniform-convergence sample-complexity logic but differ sharply in scope: VC characterises learnability via the growth function for arbitrary set systems and proves the necessary and sufficient entropy-rate condition; Valiant supplies concrete polynomial-time learning algorithms and ties learnability to computational complexity, including a cryptographic non-learnability remark. VC is purely statistical with no algorithms; Valiant has no VC dimension. Hence the relationship is best classified as parallel rediscovery (PR) of the uniform-convergence sample-complexity core, with each paper contributing a complementary piece (combinatorial dimension on one side, algorithmic learnability on the other).

matches.explanation: Both set up the underlying probability space. Valiant's DP282.3 introduces an arbitrary distribution D on positive examples {v : F(v)=1}; VC's DP283.1 introduces the elementary-event space (X, P_X) with measurable event class S. The role is the same (the unknown distribution from which samples are drawn), but VC works on the full space and an event class, whereas Valiant restricts to positive examples of one target concept.

Valiant's DP282.4 (EXAMPLES/ORACLE protocol) and VC's DP283.2 (relative frequency nu_A on a sample) both formalise the data-access model. EXAMPLES is the i.i.d. sampler that produces the size-l sample VC takes as input; the paper-282 ORACLE has no VC analogue (VC is purely passive observation).

Valiant's learnability definition DP282.5 (with probability >= 1 - h^{-1} the output g satisfies sum_{v: f(v)=1, g(v)!=1} D(v) <= h^{-1}) and VC's pi^{(l)} = sup_A |nu_A - P_A| together with the uniform-convergence definition DP283.4 are parallel formulations of approximate-learning-with-confidence. Both demand that with confidence 1-eta the deviation between target and output (Valiant) or empirical and true measure (VC) is at most epsilon, uniformly over the function class. Valiant phrases the bound only on positive examples and only one-sidedly; VC works two-sidedly over all events. Cluster-correspondence: one composite Valiant definition matches the pair of VC definitions.

Valiant's L(h,S) function (DP282.6) and its linear bound L(h,S) <= 2h(S + log h) (PrP282.1) play exactly the role of VC's explicit sample-size estimate in RP283.1: l >= (16/eps^2)(n log(2l) + log(4/eta)). Both quantify the number of samples needed for a given confidence and accuracy. Valiant phrases it via a generic coupon-collector-style function; VC phrases it via the growth function. The bounds are structurally the same (1/eps^2 times log(class size) plus log(1/eta)).

Both proofs hinge on a Chernoff/concentration argument. Valiant's PP282.1 directly invokes Chernoff's tail bound on Bernoulli trials. VC's PP283.4 uses the hypergeometric urn estimate Gamma <= 2 e^{-eps^2 l / 8} after symmetrization. Conceptually parallel exponential-tail arguments, but VC's is technically more elaborate (symmetrization + permutation averaging + growth-function reduction) while Valiant's reads off the standard Chernoff bound.

Valiant cites Chernoff's tail bound externally (TP282.cite_chernoff) and uses it inside PP282.1; VC develops its own hypergeometric Chernoff-type bound inline as part of PP283.4 (the tail estimate Gamma <= 2 e^{-eps^2 l / 8}). Cross-origin (external <-> paper) match: a result Valiant treats as cited prior work plays the same role as a step VC proves itself.

The k-CNF class (DP282.7) plays the role in Valiant of the hypothesis class whose cardinality (2t)^{k+1} controls sample complexity. VC's growth function m^S(r) (DP283.6) is the modern way to capture the same effective-class-size quantity in distribution-free learning theory. Valiant uses a hard cardinality bound on a syntactic class; VC uses a refined combinatorial measure on a set system. Conceptual role matches even though the formal objects are very different.

Valiant's Theorem A (k-CNF is learnable using L(h,(2t)^{k+1}) examples) and VC's Theorem 2 + its corollary (P{pi^{(l)} > eps} <= 4 m^S(2l) e^{-eps^2 l/8}, hence polynomial growth implies uniform convergence) are the parallel-rediscovery touchpoint of the pair. Both establish that finite-effective-complexity classes are PAC-learnable from i.i.d. samples; Valiant's proof boils down to applying his L(h,S) bound to the (2t)^{k+1} clauses, which is the cardinality-class instance of VC's growth-function bound. Many-to-many: TP282.A consumes both the bound (TP283.2) and the sufficient-condition packaging (CP283.1).

Composite L1-with-L2 alignment of the proofs of TP282.A and TP283.2. Both proofs (i) bound the number of relevant hypotheses (Valiant: (2t)^{k+1} clauses, PSP282.A1; VC: m^S(2l) essentially distinct subsamples, PSP283.9), (ii) argue soundness/measure-control on the hypothesis (Valiant: B is preserved so g => f, PSP282.A2; VC: symmetrization gives a controllable two-sample event, PSP283.8), and (iii) close with a Chernoff/hypergeometric tail bound to the desired confidence (PSP282.A3 via L(h,S); PSP283.10-11 via Gamma <= 2 e^{-eps^2 l/8}). Inner step DAGs differ in that VC's argument is symmetrization-heavy and distribution-free while Valiant's is a direct counting argument; both deliver the same shape of statement.
Algorithm A (the iterative clause-deletion learner for k-CNF from positive examples) has no VC counterpart; VC contains no learning algorithms at all, only a sample-complexity bound.

Valiant's Theorem B (monotone DNF is learnable using L(h,d) EXAMPLES + dt ORACLE calls) has no VC counterpart. The use of a membership oracle and the syntactic notion of degree d are specifically computational-learning-theoretic devices that VC does not consider.
Algorithm B (the ORACLE-driven prime-implicant learner for monotone DNF) has no VC counterpart; VC contains no learning algorithms at all.
Proof of Theorem B is specific to the prime-implicant construction and the dt-call ORACLE accounting; no VC analogue.
Theorem B' (DNF learnable on total-vector distributions) is a Valiant-specific extension involving the syntactic restriction to total inputs and the cited tautology hardness; no VC counterpart.
Valiant's corollary on bounded-disjunct DNF learnable from negative examples is a dualisation of Theorem A and is specific to the Boolean syntactic setting; no VC counterpart.

Theorem C (mu-expressions are exactly learnable in O(t^3) oracle calls) is an exact-identification result using powerful structural oracles (N-ORACLE, RP, RA), entirely in the algorithmic computational-learning regime. VC has no analogous machinery.
Algorithm C (mu-expression learner with alternating plus/times phases) is purely algorithmic; no VC counterpart.
Proof of Theorem C consists of structural induction on mu-expression depth using Claims 1-5; no VC counterpart.
Claim 1 (phase invariant on g_i) is internal to the mu-expression learner; no VC counterpart.
Claim 2 (shared completion forces shared sum) is internal to the mu-expression algorithm correctness argument; no VC counterpart.
Claim 3 (S correctly groups times-expressions) is internal to the mu-expression algorithm; no VC counterpart.
Claim 4 (T correctly groups plus-expressions) is internal to the mu-expression algorithm; no VC counterpart.
Claim 5 (depth-k subexpressions found in k phases) is internal to the mu-expression algorithm; no VC counterpart.
Open problem on learning monotone DNF from EXAMPLES alone is computational-learning-theoretic; no VC counterpart.
Definition of vector / total vector is a Boolean-domain syntactic primitive specific to Valiant; VC works in arbitrary measurable spaces and has no analogous combinatorial domain object.
Boolean function/concept extension from total to partial vectors is again a Valiant-specific Boolean object; VC studies events (measurable sets) in the abstract.
DNF expression and prime implicant are Boolean-formula primitives; no VC counterpart.
Monotone expression and degree of DNF are Boolean-syntax notions; no VC counterpart.
mu-expression is a Boolean-syntax primitive specific to Section 7 of Valiant; no VC counterpart.
The N-ORACLE / P-ORACLE / PI / RP / RA oracle hierarchy is purely a Valiant-style algorithmic-learning device; VC has no oracle model.

VC's index Delta^S(x_1,...,x_r) (the number of distinct intersection patterns of S on the sample) is the foundation of the growth-function machinery. Valiant has no analogue: he counts hypotheses syntactically rather than measuring their effective intersection complexity on a sample. This is the asymmetry that makes VC theory more general.
Phi(n,r) (the combinatorial recurrence majorising the growth function) is purely VC-internal; no Valiant counterpart since Valiant does not use a growth function at all.
Entropy H^S(l) = E[log Delta^S] of the system S, used in VC's necessary and sufficient condition (Theorem 4), has no Valiant analogue.
Two-sample deviation rho^{(l)} (the symmetrization device) is a VC-internal proof tool; no Valiant counterpart.
Lemma 1 (combinatorial dichotomy: index >= Phi(n,i) forces a shattered subsample of size n) is the Sauer-Shelah-style core of VC theory. Valiant uses no such combinatorial lemma.
Proof of Lemma 1 (induction over sample size with type-1/type-2 split) is internal to VC's growth-function dichotomy machinery; no Valiant counterpart.
Theorem 1 (growth-function dichotomy: m^S either equals 2^r or is majorised by r^n + 1) is the Sauer-Shelah lemma; no Valiant counterpart.
Proof of Theorem 1 is internal to the dichotomy result; no Valiant counterpart.
Symmetrization lemma (Lemma 2) is a VC proof tool; Valiant's proofs do not symmetrize.
Proof of Lemma 2 (Fubini + Chebyshev on the binomial) is VC-internal; no Valiant counterpart.

Theorem 3 (almost-sure uniform convergence under polynomial growth) strengthens convergence in probability to almost-sure via Borel-Cantelli. Valiant works only with finite-sample probabilistic guarantees and has no analogue.
Proof of Theorem 3 invokes Borel-Cantelli on the summable tail; no Valiant counterpart.
Subadditivity of the index logarithm is a VC-internal entropy property; no Valiant counterpart.
Existence of the entropy rate H^S(l)/l -> c via subadditivity is VC-internal; no Valiant counterpart.
Concentration of the normalized log-index around the entropy rate is VC-internal; no Valiant counterpart.
Proof of Lemma 4 (block-decomposition + Chebyshev) is VC-internal; no Valiant counterpart.

Theorem 4 (necessary and sufficient condition for uniform convergence: H^S(l)/l -> 0) is VC's deepest contribution and is genuinely distribution-dependent; Valiant has no analogue at this level of generality.
Proof of Theorem 4 (sufficiency by entropy split, necessity by shattered-subsample construction) is VC-internal; no Valiant counterpart.
